essays.stem: Describe the equipment needed to produce an engineering drawing by hand, and say how each item is used.
essays.modelAnswer: A drawing board gives a flat, smooth surface, and the paper is fixed squarely to it with clips or tape. A T-square slides along the left edge of the board to draw horizontal lines. Set squares of 45° and 30°/60° rest on the T-square to draw vertical lines and lines at 30°, 45° and 60°; used together they give 15° and 75°. A compass draws circles and arcs, and dividers transfer and step off sizes. A protractor measures and marks other angles. A scale rule is used to measure at the chosen scale. Pencils of different grades are used: a hard pencil such as 2H for light construction lines, and an H or HB pencil for outlines and lettering. A sharpener keeps the points fine, and a clean eraser and an erasing shield remove mistakes without smudging. Templates for circles and lettering help to make neat work quickly.
markingPoints: Drawing board with the paper fixed squarely
T-square for horizontal lines; set squares for vertical and angled lines
Compass, dividers and protractor for circles, sizes and angles
Scale rule for measuring at the chosen scale
Pencils of the right grades, with sharpener, eraser and shield

essays.stem: Explain why engineering drawings follow agreed rules for lines, views and dimensions, and what can go wrong if they do not.
essays.modelAnswer: Engineering drawings are read by many people: the designer, the welder, the machinist, the inspector and sometimes the customer. If everyone uses the same rules for line types, views, symbols and dimensions, a drawing means the same thing to all of them, even if they have never met. For example, a thick continuous line always means a visible edge and a dashed line a hidden edge, and the projection symbol tells the reader where each view comes from. Agreed rules also make drawings quicker to read and easier to check. If the rules are not followed, the drawing can be misread. A hidden line might be taken as a visible edge, a view might be read the wrong way round, or a size might be missed or given twice with different values. This leads to parts made wrongly, wasted material and time, parts that do not fit, and sometimes unsafe products. It can also cause arguments about who is to blame.
markingPoints: Many different people read and use the same drawing
Agreed rules make a drawing mean the same to everyone, with an example
Drawings are quicker to read and to check
If rules are broken the drawing is misread, with an example
Results: wrong parts, waste, poor fit, unsafe products or disputes

essays.stem: Explain how the views are arranged in first-angle orthographic projection, using a steel block with a slot cut in its top as an example.
essays.modelAnswer: In first-angle projection, each view is drawn on the far side of the object from where it is seen. The front view, or front elevation, is drawn first, looking at the side that shows the most about the shape. The plan, seen from above, is drawn directly below the front view. The view seen from the left is drawn to the right of the front view, and the view from the right is drawn to the left. The views are lined up, so the height is projected across from the front view to the end view, and the length is projected down from the front view to the plan. Depth is carried from the plan to the end view with a 45° line or with dividers. For a steel block with a slot in its top, the slot shows as visible lines in the plan and in any view that looks along it, and as hidden dashed lines in a view where it is behind a face. The first-angle symbol is drawn in the title block.
markingPoints: Each view is placed on the far side of the object from where it is seen
Front view chosen to show the most of the shape; plan directly below it
View from the left placed to the right of the front view
Views lined up; depth carried across with a 45° line
Slot shown as visible or hidden lines correctly; first-angle symbol in the title block

essays.stem: Describe the main rules for dimensioning an engineering drawing so that it is clear and cannot be misread.
essays.modelAnswer: All sizes are given in millimetres, and a note in the title block says so. Each size needed to make the part is given once only. Dimensions are placed outside the views where possible, between thin projection lines that start a small gap away from the outline and run a little past the dimension line. Dimension lines are thin, with neat arrowheads touching the projection lines. The number is written clearly above or in the middle of the dimension line so that it is easy to read. Smaller dimensions are placed nearer the view and larger ones further out, so lines do not cross. Dimensions are not taken to hidden lines if it can be avoided. The overall length, width and height are always given. Diameters are shown with the Ø symbol and radii with R. Where possible, sizes are taken from a datum face or edge so that errors do not add up. Where accuracy matters, a tolerance is given.
markingPoints: Sizes in millimetres; each size given once only
Outside the views, with thin projection lines (small gap) and thin dimension lines with arrowheads
Numbers clear and readable; smaller dimensions inside larger ones so lines do not cross
No dimensions to hidden lines; overall sizes always given
Ø and R used; dimensions from a datum; tolerances where needed

essays.stem: Describe how to lay out an A3 drawing sheet, including the border, the title block and the spacing of the views.
essays.modelAnswer: First I fix the A3 sheet squarely to the board. I draw a border a set distance in from the edges, often about 10 mm, first as a thin line and then lined in thick. I draw the title block in the bottom right-hand corner, with spaces for the title, drawing number, scale, projection symbol, units, material, my name, the date and the checker's name. Before drawing any views, I work out how much space each view needs at the chosen scale. I add up the widths of the front view and the end view and the gap between them, take this from the width of the drawing space, and share what is left equally on each side. I do the same with the heights of the front view and the plan. I mark these positions lightly so that the views are evenly spaced, with room for dimensions and notes, and clear of the title block. Then I draw the views with thin construction lines first.
markingPoints: Fixes the sheet squarely and draws the border
Title block in the bottom right with the main information
Works out the space each view needs at the chosen scale
Shares the spare space evenly so the views are balanced and clear of the title block
Leaves room for dimensions; starts with light construction lines

essays.stem: Describe how to make an isometric drawing of a rectangular steel block with a round hole through its top.
essays.modelAnswer: First I draw a vertical line for the nearest corner of the block, at its true height. From the bottom of this line I draw two lines at 30° to the horizontal, one to the left and one to the right, using the 30°/60° set square on the T-square. I mark the true length along one 30° line and the true width along the other. I draw vertical lines up from these points to the full height, then complete the top face with lines parallel to the 30° lines. To show the hole, I find its centre on the top face by drawing centre lines parallel to the edges. A circle on an isometric face appears as an ellipse, so I draw an isometric square around the hole, divide it with the centre lines, and construct or sketch the ellipse so it touches the middle of each side. I line in the visible edges with thick lines and leave out hidden lines, as isometric drawings usually do not show them. I add dimensions along the isometric lines if they are needed.
markingPoints: Vertical line for the nearest corner at true height
Lines at 30° each side, drawn with the 30°/60° set square
True lengths along the axes; the box completed with parallel lines
Hole drawn as an ellipse inside an isometric square on the top face
Visible edges lined in thick; hidden lines left out

essays.stem: Explain what a sectional view is, why it is used, and how it is shown on a drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: A sectional view shows an object as if it had been cut through along an imaginary plane and the front piece taken away. It is used to show inside details, such as holes, bores and wall thicknesses, which would otherwise be a confusing mass of hidden lines. A sectional view is easier to read and to dimension. On the drawing, the place where the cut is made is shown on another view by a cutting plane line. This is a thin chain line, thick at the ends and where it changes direction, with arrows showing which way the section is viewed and letters such as A–A. The sectional view is labelled with the same letters. The surfaces that have been cut are shown with thin hatching lines, usually at 45° and evenly spaced. Different parts that touch are hatched in different directions or with different spacing. Bolts, shafts and webs cut along their length are usually not hatched.
markingPoints: Definition: the object shown as if cut along a plane with the front piece removed
Purpose: shows inside details more clearly than hidden lines
Cutting plane line: thin chain, thick at the ends, arrows and letters
Cut surfaces hatched with thin lines at 45°, evenly spaced
Touching parts hatched in different directions; bolts and shafts not hatched lengthwise

essays.stem: Explain what a drawing scale is, giving examples of reduction, full-size and enlargement scales, and say how you would choose a scale for a drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: A drawing scale is the ratio between the size on the drawing and the real size of the part. It is written as drawing size : real size. A full-size drawing is 1:1. Reduction scales, such as 1:2, 1:5 and 1:10, are used for parts that are too large for the sheet. At 1:5, 1 mm on the drawing stands for 5 mm on the part. Enlargement scales, such as 2:1 or 5:1, are used for small parts so that their details can be seen. At 2:1 the drawing is twice the real size. To choose a scale, I compare the overall size of the part, with all its views, gaps and dimensions, against the space on the sheet. I choose the largest standard scale that fits, so the drawing is clear but not crowded. Whatever the scale, the dimensions written on the drawing are always the real sizes. The scale is written in the title block, and any view at a different scale is marked with its own scale.
markingPoints: A scale is the ratio of drawing size to real size
Full size 1:1, and a reduction scale explained (for example 1:5)
An enlargement scale explained (for example 2:1)
Choose the largest standard scale that fits the views, gaps and dimensions
Dimensions always show real sizes; scale stated in the title block

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to produce a finished orthographic drawing of a part, from first planning to final checking.
essays.modelAnswer: First I study the part, model or sketch and decide which view will be the front view and how many views are needed. I choose the projection method and a scale that fits the sheet. I fix the paper to the board and draw the border and title block. I plan the spacing of the views so they are evenly placed with room for dimensions. Then I draw all the views lightly with thin construction lines, starting with centre lines and the main outline of the front view, and projecting heights and lengths across to the other views. I add details such as holes, slots and hidden edges. When the views are correct, I line them in with the right line types: thick for outlines, dashed for hidden detail and chain for centre lines. I add projection lines, dimensions and notes, and fill in the title block with the scale and projection symbol. Finally I check every view and dimension against the part, correct any mistakes, clean the sheet and sign it.
markingPoints: Studies the part; chooses the front view and the number of views
Chooses projection method and scale; sets up the sheet with border and title block
Plans the spacing; draws construction lines and projects between views
Lines in with the correct line types
Adds dimensions, notes and title block details, then checks against the part

essays.stem: Compare drawing by hand with drawing on a computer (CAD). Give the advantages and disadvantages of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Drawing by hand needs only simple, cheap equipment and no electricity, so it can be done almost anywhere. It builds a good understanding of projection, and it is quick for a simple sketch or a one-off job. But it is slow for complex work, changes mean erasing and redrawing, and extra copies must be photocopied. The accuracy depends on the skill of the person drawing. Drawing with CAD needs a computer, software and training, which all cost money, and it needs power. But CAD drawings are very accurate, and the lines, text and dimensions are neat and the same every time. Changes are quick, parts can be copied and used again, and the drawing can be printed at any scale, emailed and stored safely as a file. Some CAD programs can make 3D models and send cutting paths straight to machines such as plasma cutters. Many workshops use both: a hand sketch to plan, and CAD for the final drawing.
markingPoints: Hand drawing advantages: cheap, no power needed, builds understanding, quick for simple sketches
Hand drawing disadvantages: slow for complex work, changes and copies are hard, depends on skill
CAD advantages: accurate, neat, quick to change and reuse, easy to print, send and store
CAD disadvantages: cost of computer, software and training; needs power
Conclusion: many workshops use both

practical1.title: Detail drawings of the parts of a small welded bracket in orthographic projection
practical1.brief: As a group, produce a set of drawings for a small welded steel bracket. The assessor provides a real bracket or a model, and a sketch with the main sizes. The bracket has a base plate with two holes, an upright plate and a triangular gusset. Each member produces one drawing, on A3 or A4 paper as the assessor directs, of the part they are given. In a group of 5, the fifth member draws the assembly with a parts list; in a group of 4, the group draws the assembly together. Each drawing must be in first-angle projection (or the Centre's chosen method), at a suitable scale, with a border, a title block, the projection symbol, correct line types and full dimensions in millimetres. Work in these stages: (1) as a group, measure the parts and agree the sizes; (2) each member plans their sheet layout; (3) each member draws the views in construction lines, then lines them in; (4) each member adds dimensions, notes and the title block; (5) members swap drawings, check each other's work with the assessor's checklist, and correct any errors. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: The bracket or model, and a sketch with the main sizes, from the assessor
For each member: drawing board, T-square, 45° and 30°/60° set squares, compass, protractor and scale rule
A3 or A4 drawing paper, and masking tape or clips
2H and HB pencils, eraser and sharpener
Steel rule and vernier caliper for measuring the parts
photos: The group measuring the parts and recording the sizes
A member's sheet with the border, title block and planned layout
The views drawn in construction lines
The views lined in with the correct line types
The finished, dimensioned drawing with the title block filled in
Members checking each other's drawings with the checklist
The full set of drawings laid out together
checklist: Measured the parts accurately and recorded the sizes
Fixed the paper squarely and drew the border and title block neatly
Planned the layout so the views are evenly spaced with room for dimensions
Placed the views correctly for first-angle projection (or the Centre's method), lined up with each other
Used the correct line types: thick outlines, dashed hidden detail, chain centre lines, thin dimension lines
Dimensioned the part fully and clearly in millimetres, with no size repeated
Completed the title block: title, drawing number, scale, projection symbol, material, name and date
Checked another member's drawing carefully and corrected the errors found in their own
safety: Use compass points and dividers with care, and keep them closed or covered when not in use
Keep the drawing area clear of bags and cables so nobody trips
If measuring parts in the workshop, wear safety boots and glasses and follow that area's rules
Sit with good posture and take short breaks during long drawing work

practical2.title: Isometric drawing and sectional view of a fabricated part
practical2.brief: The assessor gives each member of the group a different set of orthographic views of a simple fabricated or machined part, for example a stepped block, a flanged bush, a bracket with a hole, or a slotted base plate. Each member: (1) studies the views and plans an A3 sheet; (2) draws the part in isometric using the 30°/60° set square, with any holes drawn as ellipses; (3) draws a full sectional view of the part on the cutting plane marked by the assessor, with hatching at 45°, and shows the cutting plane line and its labels on the other view; (4) adds the main dimensions and completes the title block. Then, as a group, members pin up all the drawings and check each one against the assessor's checklist, and each member explains to the group one drawing that is not their own. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A different set of orthographic views for each member, from the assessor
Drawing board, T-square, 45° and 30°/60° set squares, compass, protractor and scale rule
A3 drawing paper, isometric grid paper for practice, and tape or clips
2H and HB pencils, eraser and sharpener
An ellipse template, if the Centre has one
The assessor's checklist and a board for pinning up drawings
photos: Each member's given views and planned sheet
The isometric drawing in construction lines
The finished isometric drawing, lined in
The sectional view with hatching and the cutting plane line
The completed sheet with dimensions and title block
The group checking the drawings pinned up together
A member explaining another member's drawing
checklist: Read the given views correctly and understood the shape
Drew the isometric axes correctly (vertical and 30°), with true lengths along them
Drew holes and curves as ellipses of the right size and in the right place
Showed the cutting plane line with arrows and labels on the correct view
Drew the sectional view correctly, with even 45° hatching on the cut surfaces only
Used the correct line types and added the main dimensions
Explained another member's drawing clearly to the group
safety: Use compass points and dividers with care, and keep them covered when not in use
Pin up drawings carefully on the board provided, and keep pins in their box
Keep walkways clear of drawing boards and bags
Take short breaks to rest your eyes and back
